passage:
Day one: at the tea stall in Patna, Sudha, four, dropped a spoon and her father Tanvir caught it before it hit the floor. She let out a low, pleased chortle. "Again!" He tossed it, caught it and she gurgled deeper.
Day three: Tanvir did a silly walk to the door and Sudha chortled at him, hand over her mouth.
Day six: Sudha herself dropped a spoon for her mother to catch, watching her face and chuckling in the same low way as her father.

qa.q: What did Sudha drop at the tea stall on day one?
qa.a: She dropped a spoon.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she chortled on day three?
qa.a: She was pleased and amused by her father's silly walk, and she covered her mouth with her hand. She may also have been enjoying the fun of sharing a game.

qa.q: What might Tanvir do to keep sharing this fun with Sudha?
qa.a: He can keep playing simple games she enjoys and laugh along with her.

qa.q: How might Sudha's mother feel when Sudha drops the spoon for her to catch?
qa.a: She may feel delighted to be part of the game, and notice that Sudha's chuckle sounds just like her father's.

grounding: A young child chortles with pleased delight when a game works, and copies the laughter style of the adults around her.

passage: The bus was stuck in a mud-slick lane after the rains near Pune, and Urmila, five, had been kept waiting so long her legs were restless. Her uncle Darshan pulled a crumpled paper hat from his pocket and put it on his head. Urmila glanced at him and let out a low chuckle that shook her shoulders. "Uncle, it's tiny!" He wiggled his ears. She gave a deep chortle, eyes shining, and the other passengers turned round and smiled. She pointed at the hat, waiting for more.

qa.q: What did Darshan take from his pocket?
qa.a: He took a crumpled paper hat from his pocket.

qa.q: What does Urmila's chuckle suggest she was feeling about the hat?
qa.a: It suggests she was amused and delighted, since her eyes were shining and she pointed at the hat for more. The wait may also have made her glad of any distraction.

qa.q: What could Darshan do next if the wait goes on?
qa.a: He can invent another small silly game, since it changed the mood for Urmila.

qa.q: How might the other passengers feel seeing this?
qa.a: They may feel warmed by Urmila's laughter, since they turned round and smiled.

grounding: A young child gives a low, pleased chortle when a joke or surprise works, showing shared enjoyment.

passage: In their flat above the chemist, Asif hid behind the long curtain. “Where's Abba?” Indu tiptoed up, yanked the curtain back, and he jumped out with a “Boo!” Indu let out a low, gurgly chortle, “Heh-heh-heh,” exactly like her father's laugh. Asif laughed too, the same low rumble. “Again!” They did it six times. Each time the chortle came at the same moment, as the curtain flew back. Her mother, cooking, said, “Two of you laughing the same way. Like father, like daughter.”

qa.q: How many times did they play the curtain game?
qa.a: Six times.

qa.q: What does Indu's low chortle each time suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt delighted and amused that the surprise worked every time, enjoying the shared game.

qa.q: What could Asif do to keep the game fun?
qa.a: He could vary where he hides now and then, so the surprise stays fresh and the chortles keep coming.

qa.q: How did Indu's mother see the laughter?
qa.a: She noticed that Indu laughed just like her father, and found it sweet and funny. 😊

grounding: A preschooler chortles with delight when a hiding game works, copying her father's laugh.

passage:
“Knock knock,” said Imran.
“Who's there?” asked Chandrika Nani.
“Banana.”
“Banana who?”
“Banana… banana…” Imran forgot the rest and chuckled low in his throat, just like Nani did.
Nani laughed. “You forgot, didn't you?”
“Heh-heh. Yes. But it's still funny.”
“Want to hear one?” Nani told the orange one. Imran chuckled again, hand over his tummy, rocking. “Tell it again, Nani!”
“Only if you tell me a new one tomorrow.”

qa.q: What joke did Nani tell Imran?
qa.a: The orange one.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he forgot the rest of his joke and chuckled?
qa.a: He felt amused and happy, enjoying the fun even without the ending. His chuckle copied Nani's laugh, which suggests he felt close to her.

qa.q: How could Nani keep this shared fun going?
qa.a: She could trade one new joke a day with Imran, as she suggested, so they both look forward to it.

qa.q: How might Nani see Imran copying her chuckle?
qa.a: She would likely feel fond and touched that he copies her laugh.

grounding: A preschooler chuckles with delight at a joke with his grandmother, copying her laughter style.

passage:
Note by Disha, preschool teacher, Thursday.
Sahil brought a coin trick to show-and-tell. He hid the coin in one fist, waved the other, and when he opened the empty hand, the class gasped. Sahil gave a low, pleased “heh heh heh,” shoulders shaking. He told me later that's how his dada laughs when a trick works. He did the trick four more times, and every time his friends shouted, he chortled again. It was lovely to see him so pleased with himself. 😊

qa.q: Where did Sahil hide the coin?
qa.a: In one fist.

qa.q: What does Sahil's low “heh heh heh” suggest he felt when the trick worked?
qa.a: It suggests he felt delighted and proud that his trick surprised everyone. He was copying his dada's laugh, which may have made him feel grown-up.

qa.q: How could Disha build on Sahil's pleasure in the trick?
qa.a: Disha could invite him to teach the trick to a small group, so the fun is shared.

qa.q: How might Sahil's friends feel when the coin disappeared?
qa.a: They felt surprised and amazed, which is why they gasped and shouted each time.

grounding: The note shows a preschooler chortling with delight when his trick works, copying his grandfather's laugh.

passage:
Behind the cowshed in the village, Ritu Bua crouched behind a haystack. "Where's Wasim? Where did he go?"

Wasim, hiding behind the water drum, pressed his hands to his mouth. Then Bua popped up right beside him. "Found you!"

Out came a low, rumbly chuckle, "heh-heh-heh", deep in his chest.

Ritu Bua laughed so hard she sat down in the straw. "That's your Dada's laugh! Exactly his!"

Wasim chuckled it again on purpose, shoulders shaking, and ran off to hide once more.

qa.q: Where was Wasim hiding?
qa.a: Behind the water drum.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when the low, rumbly chuckle came out?
qa.a: He was most likely delighted and amused that Bua found him in a surprising way. Chuckling it again on purpose shows he enjoyed the shared fun.

qa.q: How could an adult keep this kind of fun going?
qa.a: By playing along as Ritu Bua does, with more hide-and-find rounds and laughing with him, so the game stays shared and warm.

qa.q: How does Ritu Bua react to Wasim's chuckle?
qa.a: She laughs so hard she sits in the straw, delighted to hear Dada's laugh coming from the little boy.

grounding: It shows a young child's low, pleased chuckle when a game works, and how he has picked up the laughing style of an adult in the family.
